newsitem.title: GERMANY: German city takes steps against Scientology.
newsitem.headline: German city takes steps against Scientology.

text.p: The city of Stuttgart said on Wednesday it was taking measures to combat Scientology which will put it at the forefront of efforts in Germany to limit the influence of the organisation.

With immediate effect, all applicants for jobs in the city's public service will have to give an assurance in writing that they are not active members of the group, which says it is a bona fide religion but is not recognised as such in Germany, city official Juergen Kiesl told Reuters.

The treatment of Scientology in parts of Germany has attracted increasing criticism in the United States, and was raised briefly in talks between U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel.
The U.S. State Department's annual human rights report listed Scientology allegations of what it terms religious persecution in Germany, where Scientology says it has around 30,000 members.
But Kiesl, administrative head of the city's environment, security and order department, said Stuttgart was determined not to let its institutions be "undermined or infiltrated" by the group.

"For the city of Stuttgart, Scientology is not a religious community but a group which uses repressive means and employs psychological coercion to gain influence over its members and pursue economic gain," he said.

Stuttgart's move goes beyond measures taken by the state government in neighbouring Bavaria, which is asking all its job applicants to state whether or not they are Scientologists and refusing to award public contracts to firms linked to Scientology.

Anti-subversion watchdogs in Bavaria and Baden-Wuerttemberg, the regional state of which Stuttgart is the capital, already monitor Scientology for evidence that it could be seeking to undermine the democratic system. The two states are among Germany's largest, wealthiest and most conservative.
Sabine Weber, Scientology's spokeswoman in Germany, accused Stuttgart of "flagrantly abusing human rights by deciding whether or not to employ someone on the basis of the religion they belong to".

Kiesl said Stuttgart was making use of a ruling in the Federal Labour Court which allowed employers to enquire into applicants' secondary sources of earnings to see if they would interfere with the job being applied for. He said only active Scientologists would be affected by the ban.

He said Stuttgart would also exclude from public contracts any consultants, trainers or advisers who did not reject the "techniques of L. Ron Hubbard", the late American science-fiction author who founded Scientology.
